---
name: oxplow-runtime
description: How oxplow tracks your work on its own (turns and requests), handoffs between threads, and the command bus. Loads on the oxplow `run_command` tool with oxplow.handoff.*, and on v_request, v_agent_turn or v_handoff.
---

# Your work in oxplow

oxplow tracks your work without your help. Nothing here is required: no
edit or stop waits on a task, and there's nothing to close before you
finish.

- **Recorded work.** The files you change (with edit tools or a shell)
  and the test runs you make are recorded against your turn, and through
  the turn against its request. A task you start (`oxplow.task.transition`
  to in progress) or file into progress becomes yours.
- **Turns.** Each turn records what opened it (`v_agent_turn.source`: a
  person, a background job's report, a subagent, another session) and how
  it ended; `v_turn_activity` says where its time went (tools, waiting on
  the person, the rest) and its compactions. A request (`v_request`) is a
  prompt and every turn it caused, with its live state; the tasks it
  worked on are `v_request_task`.
- **Session history.** In SQL the history of your conversations is
  `v_agent_session` (the slots opened on a thread), `v_agent_session_status`
  (each open session's last status), `v_agent_turn` (each prompt and
  answer), `v_tool_call` and `v_subagent`; the tasks a session's requests
  worked on are `v_request_task` joined to `v_task`. A session that lost its
  conversation is brought back with `oxplow.agent_session.reopen { session }`;
  the transcript page offers it.
- **Standing instructions.** What the person set for every session of
  your stream and of your thread is `v_stream.prompt` and `v_thread.prompt`
  (`SELECT s.prompt, t.prompt FROM v_thread t JOIN v_stream s ON s.id =
  t.stream_id`); they are already in your system prompt.
- **Waiting on the person.** When you need their answer, end your reply
  with the question: oxplow shows your thread as waiting on them. Nothing
  else is needed.
- **Handoffs.** Work another thread hands you arrives at the start of a
  prompt in a `<handoffs>` block. Take it on or decline it with
  `oxplow.handoff.resolve`; to hand work to another thread, see
  `references/commands.md`. Nothing wakes the other agent.
- **Context basket.** A `<context-basket>` block is what the person
  collected for you; read each `[oxplow uri …]` with `oxplow_read`.
- **Hints.** oxplow may add short, advisory guidance to your next prompt
  or tool result (work grown large with nothing committed, metric movement).

## Writing about work

Refer to a task by its quoted title, never by id or "#N": the person
can't map ids to what they see. Write entities in task bodies, summaries
and wiki pages as `[[…]]` wikilinks (syntax: the oxplow-wiki-capture skill).
Inline code is for identifiers and snippets.

# Commands (the one write path)

State changes are **commands**. `list_commands` lists what you may run (ids
and summaries); `list_commands { id }` (or `{ prefix: "oxplow.handoff." }`)
shows a command's input schema and an example input: read it before a
command's first run and copy the example's shape. `run_command { id, input }`
runs one. Every run is validated, policy-checked and audited; undoable runs
return an `inverse`.

Invalid input names the failing field, what it accepts and the example
input; a denial says why. A run that needs the person's confirmation
returns `{ kind: "proposed", proposal, message }` and waits in their
Alerts. Tell them what you proposed and why; don't run it again or look
for another way to make the change.

`references/commands.md`: project config keys (`oxplow.config.*`, and which
need confirmation), the families of commands, offloading a read-heavy
question to an Explore subagent through a note, and handing work to
another thread.

name: track-work
description: How to keep oxtask, the project's task tracker, showing what you work on — take or file a task when you start something new, move it to in progress at once, and to done only when it is fully done. Loads at the start of any work that will change files, and on the oxplow `run_command` tool with oxplow.task.transition or oxplow.task.create.
---

# Track your work as tasks

The person follows what each thread works on in its Work panel and on the
Work board. Both show tasks, and nothing else: a turn or a prompt is not on
them. Keep them true.

## When you start something new

Something new is work the person will want to see as one item: a feature,
a fix, a refactor, an investigation that ends in a change. A question
answered, a one-line fix or a command run is not: it needs no task.

1. Look for the task that already says it: the thread's own
   (`oxplow_thread_tasks { thread }`), then the open ones
   (`SELECT uri, title, state FROM v_task WHERE state NOT IN ('done','canceled')`
   through `oxplow_query_sql`, or `oxplow_search` with kind `task`).
2. None says it: file one (`oxplow.task.create`, the `tasks` skill), a
   title the person would recognize.
3. Move it to `in_progress` before you edit:

```json
{ "id": "oxplow.task.transition",
  "input": { "uri": "<the task's uri>", "to": "in_progress" } }
```

That also takes it: it's assigned to your thread, and the Work panel shows
it under "In progress" at once.

## While you work

One task in progress at a time per thread is the norm. When the work moves
to something else, move the first task back (`todo`, or `blocked` with a
comment that says why) before you start the next. Work that belongs to an
epic is its child task, not the epic.

## When it is done

Move it to `done` when it is fully done: the change is made, tests pass,
and it is committed if the project commits. Not when a step is done, and
not when you stop to ask the person something. If the person stops it,
`canceled`.

```json
{ "id": "oxplow.task.transition", "input": { "uri": "<the task's uri>", "to": "done" } }
```

oxplow links each task to the requests that worked on it from what it
observes; you never report that.
